title: Before sunrise and sunset
hookLine: be patient and glorify before sunrise and before sunset (20:130)

lines: THE FIRST MINUTES, THE LAST LIGHT.
cards: A day has two edges. The first few minutes after you wake, before the world gets in. And the last stretch of afternoon light, when the shadows go long.
Everything else sits in between. Near its end, Ta-Ha tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who is hearing hard words from his opponents, what to do at both edges. It starts with patience.

teach.b: Verse one hundred thirty, in Pickthall's words: bear with what they say, "and celebrate the praises of thy Lord ere the rising of the sun and ere the going down thereof."

teach.h: SABBIH: SAY GOD IS FAR ABOVE FAULT.
teach.b: The verb is sabbih: glorify, say subhan Allah, God is far above every fault. That's tasbih, the same root as the opening of Al-Isra, glory to Him who carried His servant by night.
The verse adds more times: some hours of the night, and the ends of the day. Like the dawn verse in Al-Isra a couple of weeks back, commentators read it as a map of the prayer times.
Before sunrise is Fajr. Before sunset is 'Asr, the afternoon prayer. The hours of the night hold Maghrib and 'Isha.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim singles out the two edges: the Prophet said that whoever prays before the rising of the sun and before its setting will not enter the Fire.

teach.h: LA'ALLAKA TARDA: THAT YOU BE CONTENT.
teach.b: Then the verse gives a reason, la'allaka tarda: so that you may be content, well pleased. That's the surprise. The command ends not in duty or reward, but in contentment.
The man being mocked is told: glorify at both ends of the day, and you'll find peace.
Beyond the prayers, some Muslims keep morning and evening remembrances, the adhkar, short phrases said as the day opens and as it closes.
One of the simplest, from a hadith in Bukhari: subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, glory to God and praise to Him. Ta-Ha opened by saying the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out.
It closes by framing the day with praise at both edges, so the middle, with all its hard words, can be borne.

how: Muslims pray Fajr before sunrise and 'Asr before sunset among the five daily prayers, and some recite the morning and evening adhkar, including subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, at the two ends of the day.

o: the dawn prayer said before the sun comes up
glorifying God: saying He is far above every fault
a plea for forgiveness said at the end of the day

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: so that you may be content

s: 20:130 ends with a promise of contentment
la'allaka tarda: so that you may be well pleased.
tasbih in 20:130 shares a root with the opening of Al-Isra
sabbih and subhana: glory, God far above every fault.
commentators see no prayer times in this verse
they read Fajr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha in it.

games.q: people are saying hurtful things about you every day. what does 20:130 tell the Prophet to do first?
o: bear with what they say, and glorify God before sunrise and before sunset.
games.why: patience, then praise at both edges of the day, so that you may be content.

practice: Wherever you are in your day, sit and say it once, slowly, aloud or under your breath: subhan Allah. If you're not Muslim, sit with the plain meaning: glory beyond anything I can name.
Then picture the two edges ahead, this evening's last light and tomorrow's first minutes, and let the word wait there for them.

wordCard.voice: Tasbih. Glorifying God at the two edges of the day, with patience in between, so that you may be content. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: glory be to God, the tasbih, from the root of sabbih in 20:130.

carryVoice: Your line: glory at both edges. The middle of the day is for patience. That's Ta-Ha, start to finish.

sources.q: and celebrate the praises of thy Lord ere the rising of the sun and ere the going down thereof.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 634 (whoever prays before sunrise and before sunset)
